Tokenizer-induced domain shift in cross-lingual transfer asks: when a multilingual model's tokenizer was trained on one corpus distribution and fine-tuning happens on a different one, does the representational bottleneck change in ways that corrupt transfer — and if so, through what mechanism? The key concepts are subword fertility (average tokens per word for a given language/domain), vocabulary coverage (the fraction of word types in the fine-tuning corpus that appear as single tokens versus fragmented), and the embedding lookup geometry that gets activated at each layer. A beginner sees fertility as a performance proxy — "high fertility means bad tokenization" — but an expert worries about something more insidious: differential fertility shift, where fertility increases sharply for the target language but stays flat for the source, meaning the two languages now inhabit structurally different positions in the sequence length distribution, breaking the implicit length-normalized attention patterns the model internalized during pretraining. The deeper danger is that fine-tuning on the low-resource target language then updates shared subword embeddings in ways that are geometrically coherent for the high-fertility regime but destructive for the source language's lower-fertility regime — a form of cross-lingual representation collapse that looks like ordinary forgetting but is actually tokenizer-mediated. Experts also worry about the asymmetry in gradient signal: fragmented tokens receive diluted gradient updates because the loss is averaged over more positions, so fine-tuning on a high-fertility language systematically undertrains the embeddings that matter most for low-fertility reconstruction.

Shared subword pieces — morphological fragments like "ing", "##ción", or script-universal byte-pair units — serve dual representational roles: in low-fertility languages they often encode nearly complete morphemes with rich semantic content, while in high-fertility languages they encode partial, context-incomplete fragments whose meaning is compositionally resolved across many adjacent tokens. During fine-tuning on a high-fertility target language, gradient updates push shared embedding vectors toward representations optimized for the fragment role — carrying weak, position-dependent signals that expect neighboring tokens to complete the meaning — because that is the dominant context in which those pieces appear in the fine-tuning loss. Pires et al. (2019) attributed multilingual BERT's cross-lingual transfer to shared subword overlap, but Conneau et al. (2020) with XLM-R showed that this sharing is a double-edged sword: the "curse of multilinguality" emerges precisely because shared embedding capacity gets pulled toward the language with the highest token frequency, which in high-fertility domains is the fragmented target. Concretely, if Finnish or Turkish (fertility often 2–4× English on standard BPE vocabularies) dominates fine-tuning batches, the embedding for a piece like "talo" shifts from encoding a semantically grounded nominal root toward encoding a high-uncertainty prefix state, degrading its utility when the source language (say, English) uses that same piece as a complete, low-ambiguity token. The update direction is problematic not because it is wrong for the target language but because the gradient has no mechanism to distinguish the functional role the piece plays per-language — the embedding is a single vector that must serve both roles simultaneously, and fine-tuning collapses that ambiguity in favor of whichever role dominates the loss landscape. Rust et al. (2021) demonstrated this empirically by showing that models with language-specific tokenizers substantially outperform shared-vocabulary models on morphologically rich languages, precisely because shared pieces carry conflated gradient signals during multilingual fine-tuning.

Freezing shared subword embeddings during fine-tuning yields a nuanced and revealing result: cross-lingual transfer typically improves for morphologically rich target languages on tasks like NER and POS tagging, but degrades for tasks requiring deep semantic composition like NLI or reading comprehension — a dissociation that immediately localizes the damage. Pfeiffer et al. (2021) with MAD-X and adapter-based fine-tuning showed that freezing the base model (including embeddings) while inserting language-specific adapters preserved source-language structure well enough to enable strong zero-shot transfer, effectively confirming that unfrozen fine-tuning was corrupting the shared embedding space, not just the upper layers. However, the degradation on semantic tasks when embeddings are frozen reveals the second propagation site: the transformer's attention layers have learned, during pretraining, positional and contextual integration patterns calibrated to specific fertility regimes, so feeding them frozen low-fertility embeddings in high-fertility sequence contexts creates a structural mismatch — the attention heads apply span-integration strategies optimized for longer token sequences to inputs that don't require that integration, producing over-smoothed representations. Artetxe et al. (2020) demonstrated a complementary finding by showing that re-initializing and retraining only the embedding layer of a monolingual model on a new language while freezing all transformer weights still achieved competitive cross-lingual transfer — suggesting the transformer layers themselves encode surprisingly language-agnostic computation, but only when the embedding interface respects the fertility distribution they were trained on. This means fertility-induced damage propagates through two distinct channels: the embedding collision channel (shared vectors pulled toward fragment-role representations) and the attention calibration channel (layer-wise integration patterns misapplied to structurally alien sequence length distributions), and freezing embeddings fixes the first while exposing the second. The practical implication is that neither full fine-tuning nor full freezing is correct — the damage requires surgical intervention at both sites simultaneously, which is precisely what language-specific adapter stacks with learned embedding projections attempt to achieve.

Increasing fine-tuning sequence length to compensate for higher fertility does not resolve the misalignment and in fact introduces a compounding problem: positional encodings in models like mBERT or XLM-R encode not just order but implicitly encode semantic density expectations — the model learned during pretraining that position k in a sequence carries roughly a certain amount of propositional content, calibrated to the fertility distribution of the pretraining corpus. When a high-fertility language expands the same propositional content across more token positions, the positional encodings now label semantically thin fragments with position indices that the model associates with semantically rich units, creating a density mismatch that attention cannot self-correct because the query-key dot products are computed over the same misaligned representations. Press et al. (2022) with ALiBi and Su et al. (2024) with RoPE both show that length generalization is already fragile within a single language — models trained at length 512 degrade measurably at 1024 even in monolingual settings — and cross-lingual fertility divergence adds a second axis of mismatch on top of this known fragility, so the extended positions are both out-of-distribution and semantically miscalibrated. Empirically, Adelani et al. (2022) in the MasakhaNER work found that simply padding or extending context for high-fertility African languages did not recover the performance gap relative to English, and ablations suggested the problem was not insufficient context but misaligned token-level representations — consistent with a density mismatch hypothesis rather than a length hypothesis. The deeper issue is that span boundaries — the positions where attention heads have learned to execute aggregation versus routing operations — no longer align with morpheme or word boundaries in the high-fertility language, so increasing length just gives the model more misaligned positions to integrate over, amplifying rather than correcting the structural conflict. What actually helps, as demonstrated in work on token merging and subword regularization (Kudo 2018, with BPE-dropout), is reducing fertility variance during fine-tuning rather than accommodating its consequences — keeping the token-to-morpheme ratio closer to the pretraining distribution so that positional and attentional patterns fire at the semantic granularity they were calibrated for.

When the same syntactic structure is encoded in a high-fertility language, attention rollout (Abnar & Zuidema 2020) reveals that these syntactically specialized heads distribute their attention mass across the expanded token span representing a single word, effectively averaging over fragment embeddings rather than attending to a single semantically coherent anchor — the head's implicit "find the syntactic head of this phrase" operation degrades into "find the most informative fragment among several semantically incomplete ones," which is a categorically different computation. Chi et al. (2020) probed mBERT's syntactic representations cross-lingually and found that syntactic structure transfer degrades systematically with morphological complexity, with dependency parsing accuracy on high-fertility languages like Arabic and Turkish lagging 8–15 F1 points behind low-fertility languages even when syntactic structures are parallel — a gap that cannot be explained by vocabulary mismatch alone and aligns with the span-boundary misalignment hypothesis. The activation pattern difference is not merely quantitative: high-fertility inputs cause syntactic heads to exhibit higher entropy attention distributions (more diffuse, less peaked), which Voita et al. (2019) identified as the signature of heads that have lost their functional specialization — in their pruning experiments, high-entropy heads were the ones safely removable without performance loss, meaning fertility misalignment is effectively functionally lobotomizing syntactically specialized heads. This implies that fine-tuning on high-fertility data doesn't just degrade token representations — it actively disrupts the functional circuit organization that multilingual pretraining established, with downstream consequences for any task requiring syntactic mediation.

The damage is partially permanent and partially reversible, and the decomposition of those two components is itself mechanistically informative. The reversible component is large: when you feed a fine-tuned model low-fertility inputs, the syntactically specialized heads recover much of their peaked attention structure, confirming that a significant portion of the entropy increase is input-distribution-driven rather than weight-encoded — the head's query and key matrices still encode the right inductive bias, they just receive fragment embeddings that produce diffuse similarity scores. However, Michel et al. (2019) demonstrated that attention heads can be permanently pruned away with minimal loss after fine-tuning on task-specific data, which implies that fine-tuning does reshape weight matrices, not just activation statistics — and Merchant et al. (2020) showed via representational similarity analysis that fine-tuning on downstream tasks causes measurable geometric drift in the weight space of middle layers, with earlier layers more stable and later layers more plastic, meaning the permanent damage concentrates in layers 6–10 of a 12-layer model where syntactic heads are densest. The permanent component manifests as a subtle but consequential shift in the query-key subspace: high-fertility fine-tuning updates Q and K matrices to better distinguish fragment-level features — morphological boundaries, byte-level patterns — at the expense of word-level syntactic feature discrimination, because the gradient signal during fine-tuning was dominated by fragment-to-fragment attention decisions. Mosbach et al. (2021) found that catastrophic forgetting in fine-tuned BERT follows a layer-wise pattern consistent with this — probing accuracy for syntactic properties drops most sharply in middle layers after fine-tuning, and this drop is only partially recovered by re-exposing the model to the original data distribution, with a residual 3–7 point probe accuracy deficit that persists. This permanent residual is best understood as the weight matrices having learned a new Pareto compromise between fragment-role and morpheme-role attention — not fully optimized for either, but shifted toward the fine-tuning distribution in a way that cannot be undone by inference-time input changes alone.

Yes, and this inspection approach constitutes one of the most diagnostically powerful tools available for understanding fertility-induced transfer failure. The adapter's down-projection matrix — the first linear transformation that compresses the residual stream from model dimension to bottleneck dimension — learns to selectively amplify directions in activation space that the diffuse attention underweighted; by projecting the adapter's weight matrix onto probing classifiers trained for specific syntactic relations, you can read off which dependency types the adapter is compensating for most heavily, effectively using the adapter as an involuntary diagnostic instrument. Chronopoulou et al. (2021) showed that adapter weight matrices trained on typologically different languages cluster by morphological complexity rather than language family, which implies the adapters are encoding something systematic about the fertility-induced representational gap — and a natural extension is to correlate the magnitude of adapter activation for specific token positions with per-arc dependency parsing errors, which Glavas & Vulic (2021) approached indirectly by showing that cross-lingual transfer errors on parsing concentrate on long-distance arcs and arcs crossing clause boundaries. The residual signal from diffuse attention predictably degrades arc types in a specific order: head-dependent arcs spanning multiple words (subject-verb, relative clause attachment) degrade first because they require the model to maintain a coherent word-level representation across several fragment tokens before the arc can be resolved, while local arcs (determiner-noun, auxiliary-verb in head-final languages) degrade less because they can be partially recovered from positional proximity even with diffuse attention. This ordering is consistent with the span-length hypothesis: an arc spanning n words in a low-fertility language spans roughly n × fertility-ratio tokens in a high-fertility language, and the probability of attention diffusion causing arc-resolution failure scales with that expanded span, making long-distance dependencies a direct casualty of fertility mismatch in a quantitatively predictable way. The most underexplored opportunity here is using the adapter's learned compensation direction as a supervision signal — if the adapter reliably recovers subject-verb arc information that diffuse attention lost, you could distill that recovery operation back into the main model's Q/K matrices via targeted fine-tuning, closing the loop between diagnostic inspection and architectural repair.
